name: Electric blankets and heating pads

comps.spec: Long flexible heating wire. A plug-in Sunbeam blanket averaged 41 W on its highest setting in a lab (Aijazi sleep); a 12 V travel blanket is labelled 50 W, under 4.5 A (12 V blanket sheet). Read your blanket's label
comps.loc: Sewn through the blanket in channels

comps.spec: Fleece or polyester blanket — still warm with the power off
Triac or relay switching the heat

notes:
A 12V blanket warms a person for a fraction of the power a space heater uses on the whole room.

Measured: a heated blanket on its highest setting averaged 41 W in a 16 °C room and warmed a sleeping manikin as much as making the room about 4.5 °C warmer (Aijazi sleep). A 12 V travel blanket is labelled 50 W, under 4.5 A, with an 8 A fuse (12 V blanket sheet). Plan on about 40–60 W a person, which brackets those two figures, but read your own blanket's label.

Blankets and pads burn people who can't feel heat or move away from it. Sunbeam says not to use its heated bedding with an infant or child, a paraplegic or quadriplegic person, anyone incapacitated or immobile, a diabetic, or anyone insensitive to heat, such as a person with poor circulation (Sunbeam heated bedding). Check the blanket's manual before running a mains blanket from an inverter or generator: Sunbeam says not to use its heated bedding with generators, power converters or inverters (Sunbeam heated bedding).
